title: Birth Order and Fate: Temporal Identity and the Inside-Out Cortex

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: A late-born excitatory neuron in the developing mammalian cortical plate reaches earlier-born neurons but cannot pass them. What happens to its expected layer position, and why?
cards.back: It fails to reach its normal position above those earlier neurons. Inside-out construction requires later cortical-plate neurons to pass earlier ones.
cards.quote: So the late neurons must travel past the early ones to reach the top.

cards.front: A radial glial progenitor in the embryonic cortex sends a long fibre to the {{c1::pia}}.
cards.back: The pia is at the outer surface.
cards.quote: Many of its progenitors are radial glia, which divide and send a long fibre up to the pia
cards.section: The layout

cards.front: The mammalian cortical plate becomes layers {{c1::2 to 6}}.
cards.back: Layer 1 comes from the early preplate.
cards.quote: The cortical plate is where the neurons settle, and it becomes layers 2 to 6.
cards.section: The layout

cards.front: Why does a cortical neuron's birthday record its temporal identity rather than cause it?
cards.back: The birthday is a timestamp. The progenitor's competence and the cues it reads at that time set temporal identity.
cards.quote: The state has two parts: what the progenitor can still make (its competence) and the cues it reads.
cards.section: The layout

cards.front: Thymidine birth-dating dates a neuron's final {{c1::S phase}}.
cards.back: This is the DNA-copying phase of the cell that divides to make the neuron.
cards.quote: To date a neuron's birth, you date its last S phase, the part of the cell cycle when DNA is copied.
cards.section: Dating a birthday

cards.front: Why does a short pulse of labeled thymidine mark only some cells in a developing brain?
cards.back: Only cells copying DNA while the label is available incorporate it; thymidine is used in DNA.
cards.quote: Only DNA uses thymidine, so only cells copying DNA in the next hour or so are marked.
cards.section: Dating a birthday

cards.front: Why are lightly labeled neurons poor markers of the cohort born immediately after a thymidine pulse?
cards.back: Extra divisions dilute the label. Lightly labeled neurons can leave the cycle at several later times, so they do not identify one birth cohort.
cards.quote: they were born later than the pulse, at many times.
cards.section: Dating a birthday

cards.front: A labeled progenitor divides to produce a neuron immediately after a thymidine pulse. Relative to that neuron's label, what percentage remains in a lineage that undergoes three extra divisions before cycle exit? Assume no later label uptake.
cards.back: Each extra division halves the label: (1/2)^3 = 1/8 = 12.5% of the reference label.
cards.quote: A daughter that leaves the cycle at that division keeps the most label, and each extra division halves it.
cards.section: Dating a birthday

cards.front: Two brief DNA-labeling pulses mark earlier and later cohorts in developing cortical tissue. Later examination finds the earlier heavily labeled cohort deeper. Does this support addition beneath existing neurons or passage above them?
cards.back: Passage above existing neurons. Adding new neurons beneath old ones would instead push the earlier cohort toward the surface.
cards.quote: Cells labeled earliest lay deepest, beside the white matter, and cells labeled on later days lay progressively nearer the surface.
cards.section: Dating a birthday

cards.front: Why does the preplate prevent applying 'earlier, deeper' to every neuron in the developing mammalian cortex?
cards.back: The cortical plate splits the early preplate. Its cells remain above as marginal zone and below as subplate, outside the cortical plate's inside-out sequence.
cards.quote: The preplate's cells are born first, yet they end up both at the top, in the marginal zone, and at the bottom, in the subplate.
cards.section: Dating a birthday

cards.front: An early thymidine pulse heavily labels neurons later found near the pia. Before rejecting inside-out development, what anatomical distinction must you check?
cards.back: Check whether they occupy the marginal zone or the cortical plate. Heavy label dates their final S phase; the preplate rule permits early-born marginal-zone cells above the later cortical plate. Within the cortical plate, earlier-born neurons tend to lie deeper.
cards.quote: "Earlier, deeper" holds inside the cortical plate.
cards.section: Dating a birthday

cards.front: Early ferret cortical donors contain labeled cells still in S phase and others already late in the cycle. Both are grafted into an older upper-layer-stage host. Predict the difference among daughters that reach cortex, and why.
cards.back: S-phase donors mostly produce upper-layer daughters; late-cycle donors mostly produce deep-layer daughters. The host can influence the first group before commitment, whereas the second group has already committed.
cards.quote: Cells moved later in the cycle mostly settled in the deep layers, out of step with the host.
cards.section: Cause or record? Moving a birthday

cards.front: How precisely do the ferret grafts locate commitment to laminar fate within the final cell cycle?
cards.back: They bracket commitment after S phase and before division as a working model; they do not demonstrate one precise switch.
cards.quote: The grafts do not show a single switch, so treat "after S phase, before mitosis" as a working model.
cards.section: Cause or record? Moving a birthday

cards.front: A late ferret cortical progenitor encounters deep-layer cues in a young host before its final division. Would encountering those cues before commitment alone restore deep-layer output, and why?
cards.back: No. Late ferret progenitors have lost deep-layer competence, so early access to those cues alone is insufficient; they still make upper-layer neurons.
cards.quote: They had lost deep-layer fates from their menu, so they could not answer the young host's cues.
cards.section: Cause or record? Moving a birthday

cards.front: How could you distinguish a fixed intrinsic fate schedule from environmental influence in developing neural progenitors while controlling for donor age?
cards.back: Split same-age donors between younger and older hosts before commitment, then compare daughter fates. A host-dependent difference supports environmental influence. The relevant rules are that cues act before commitment and donor competence limits responses.
cards.quote: Both: the host's cues count until the cell commits, and what the progenitor can still make narrows with age.
cards.section: Cause or record? Moving a birthday

cards.front: In most embryonic Drosophila nerve-cord neuroblasts, the temporal-factor sequence is Hunchback → {{c1::Krüppel}} → Pdm → Castor.
cards.back: The expression windows overlap.
cards.quote: most neuroblasts express four factors in turn: Hunchback, then Krüppel, then Pdm, then Castor.
cards.section: What a clock is made of: the fly

cards.front: How does a ganglion mother cell preserve a temporal state from a Drosophila neuroblast?
cards.back: It retains the temporal factor present when it buds off; its neurons retain that factor too.
cards.quote: A ganglion mother cell keeps the factor that was on when it budded off, and so do its neurons.
cards.section: What a clock is made of: the fly

cards.front: In the idealized Drosophila NB7-1 lineage, which factor combination distinguishes U5 from U4?
cards.back: U5 corresponds to Pdm plus Castor; U4 corresponds to Pdm alone.
cards.quote: U5 needs the overlap: Pdm alone goes with U4, Pdm together with Castor with U5.
cards.section: What a clock is made of: the fly

cards.front: Hunchback is prolonged in two Drosophila neuroblast lineages that normally make different first-born neuron types. Must their extra early-type neurons now match each other, and why?
cards.back: No. Each lineage repeats its own first-born type. Spatial lineage identity sets the class, while the Hunchback window selects early members within that class.
cards.quote: Hunchback did not make every first-born cell the same; each lineage made its own first-born type.
cards.section: What a clock is made of: the fly

cards.front: Why is altering Hunchback in the Drosophila nervous system stronger evidence for temporal specification than observing its normal expression sequence?
cards.back: Removing Hunchback loses first-born identities in tested lineages; prolonging it repeats early identities. Perturbing identity supports causation rather than expression alone.
cards.quote: Expression in sequence is a correlation. To show the factors set identity, take one away or keep it on too long.
cards.section: What a clock is made of: the fly

cards.front: A Drosophila ganglion mother cell buds off during a Hunchback window. Only the parent neuroblast is then forced into a later factor state. Would the earlier daughter's temporal identity necessarily advance, and why?
cards.back: No. Under the stated inheritance rule, the ganglion mother cell retains its budding-time factor. Combined with the rule that temporal factors specify identity, this predicts preservation of its earlier temporal state despite the parent's later change.
cards.quote: A ganglion mother cell keeps the factor that was on when it budded off, and so do its neurons.
cards.section: What a clock is made of: the fly

cards.front: In the two-outcome progenitor model, Q is the fraction of {{c1::daughters}} that leave the cycle to become neurons.
cards.back: Q is the leaving fraction.
cards.quote: Each daughter either divides again (the proliferative fraction, P) or leaves the cycle to become a neuron (the leaving fraction, Q).
cards.section: How many of each: the Q schedule

cards.front: In a two-outcome progenitor model with proliferative fraction P and leaving fraction Q, P + Q = {{c1::1}}.
cards.back: Every daughter either keeps cycling or leaves to become a neuron.
cards.quote: Each daughter either divides again (the proliferative fraction, P) or leaves the cycle to become a neuron (the leaving fraction, Q).
cards.section: How many of each: the Q schedule

cards.front: Why is Q = 0.5 the boundary between growth and shrinkage of a progenitor pool in the two-daughter model?
cards.back: Each mother produces two daughters. Keeping half cycling replaces each mother once; a smaller leaving fraction expands the pool, and a larger one shrinks it.
cards.quote: When Q is below 0.5 the pool grows; at 0.5 it holds; above 0.5 it shrinks.
cards.section: How many of each: the Q schedule

cards.front: In the two-outcome model, 250 progenitors each divide once with Q = 0.4. With no cell death, how many cycling progenitors and new neurons remain?
cards.back: Daughters = 2 × 250 = 500. Neurons = 0.4 × 500 = 200. Cycling progenitors = (1 − 0.4) × 500 = 300.
cards.quote: Progenitors after one cycle = 2 × P × progenitors before. Neurons made in that cycle = 2 × Q × progenitors before.
cards.section: How many of each: the Q schedule

cards.front: Start with 200 progenitors in the two-outcome model. Q is 0.25 for one cycle, then 0.75 for the next. Each progenitor divides once per cycle, with no cell death. What are the final cycling pool and total new neurons?
cards.back: Cycle 1: 400 daughters → 300 cycling + 100 neurons. Cycle 2: 600 daughters → 150 cycling + 450 neurons. Final pool = 150; total neurons = 100 + 450 = 550.
cards.quote: Progenitors after one cycle = 2 × P × progenitors before. Neurons made in that cycle = 2 × Q × progenitors before.
cards.section: How many of each: the Q schedule

cards.front: A two-outcome progenitor pool starts at 150 cells. Q is 0.5, then 0.7 in consecutive cycles. With one division per progenitor per cycle and no death, does neuron output peak when pool growth stops? Calculate both outputs and the final pool.
cards.back: No. Using 2QN for neuron output and 2(1 − Q)N for the next pool: cycle 1 makes 150 neurons and leaves 150 progenitors; cycle 2 makes 210 neurons and leaves 90 progenitors. Output rises by 210/150 = 1.4 despite subsequent pool shrinkage.
cards.quote: Here, just past 0.5 the pool shrinks slowly while Q climbs, so output rises
cards.section: How many of each: the Q schedule

cards.front: Why can't neuron output from the Q model be read directly as the final size of a cortical layer?
cards.back: Q counts daughters leaving the cycle, not their identities. The model does not assign each output cohort to a particular layer.
cards.quote: The model counts how many daughters leave, not which identity they take, so do not read its output as the sizes of the layers.
cards.section: How many of each: the Q schedule

cards.front: In the two-outcome progenitor model, a nonempty pool has Q = 0.8 in its final simulated cycle. Is the cycling pool exhausted, and why?
cards.back: No. Some daughters still cycle because Q is below 1. Under this model's rules, complete exhaustion requires Q = 1 in a cycle.
cards.quote: In this two-outcome model the pool would empty only in a cycle with Q = 1
cards.section: How many of each: the Q schedule

cards.front: Why does the mouse ventricular-zone Q model omit some divisions that contribute cortical neurons?
cards.back: It follows ventricular-zone progenitors only. Subventricular intermediate progenitors add divisions that the model does not track.
cards.quote: It describes the ventricular zone only; intermediate progenitors in the subventricular zone add divisions of their own that the model does not follow.
cards.section: How many of each: the Q schedule

cards.front: In mouse cortex, {{c1::Tbr1}} is high in subplate and layer 6 neurons.
cards.back: Marker expression overlaps between classes.
cards.quote: In mouse, Tbr1 is high in subplate and layer 6 neurons
cards.section: What a birthday leaves behind

cards.front: Which two markers are high in mouse layer 5 neurons that project below the cortex?
cards.back: Ctip2 and Fezf2.
cards.quote: Ctip2 and Fezf2 are high in layer 5 neurons that project below the cortex
cards.section: What a birthday leaves behind

cards.front: In mouse cortex, {{c1::Satb2}} marks callosal neurons, mostly in upper layers.
cards.back: Callosal neurons send axons to the other hemisphere.
cards.quote: Satb2 marks callosal neurons, which send axons to the other hemisphere and are mostly in the upper layers.
cards.section: What a birthday leaves behind

cards.front: What neurotransmitter contrast distinguishes cortical excitatory projection neurons from inhibitory interneurons?
cards.back: The excitatory neurons release glutamate; inhibitory interneurons release GABA.
cards.quote: The schedule in this lesson describes the excitatory, glutamate-releasing neurons made by dorsal progenitors.
cards.section: What a birthday leaves behind

cards.front: Where are most cortical GABA-releasing interneurons born in rodents?
cards.back: In the ganglionic eminences of the ventral telencephalon; they migrate into the cortex.
cards.quote: born in rodents in the ganglionic eminences, bulges in the floor of the forebrain (the ventral telencephalon)
cards.section: What a birthday leaves behind

cards.front: A manipulation leaves a mouse cortical neuron deep in the cortical plate, but it expresses Satb2. Can deep position alone establish that it acquired a deep-layer identity? What additional evidence is needed?
cards.back: No. Position alone does not define class, and Satb2 is associated with mostly upper-layer callosal neurons. Combining those rules, assess additional identity markers and projection pattern; overlapping expression means one marker cannot settle the classification.
cards.quote: Expression overlaps, and position alone does not define a class.
cards.section: What a birthday leaves behind

cards.front: Isolated mouse cortical progenitor clones make neurons with early deep-layer markers before later markers. What does their order support?
cards.back: A temporal schedule carried within the lineage: normal cortical surroundings are not required for the observed order in culture.
cards.quote: clones made neurons with early, deep-layer markers before neurons with later markers.
cards.section: Does a mammal run a clock like the fly's?

cards.front: Do ordered marker production in isolated mouse cortical clones and cue-responsive ferret grafts together establish a fly-like transcription-factor cascade in cortex?
cards.back: No. Clone order supports a lineage schedule, while grafts show cues can influence uncommitted cells within their competence. Those rules allow intrinsic and environmental contributions without specifying a molecular cascade; a complete fly-like cortical cascade remains unshown.
cards.quote: A full cascade like the fly's has not been shown in cortex.
cards.section: Does a mammal run a clock like the fly's?

cards.front: What feature of thymidine accounts for its incorporation into DNA rather than RNA during birth-dating?
cards.back: Its deoxyribose sugar.
cards.quote: Its deoxyribose sugar is why it goes into DNA and not RNA.
cards.section: Why only DNA takes up the label

cards.front: If Seven-up function is lost in an embryonic Drosophila neuroblast, what temporal-identity bias would you predict, and why?
cards.back: A bias toward repeated early identities, if Hunchback consequently stays on longer. Seven-up is needed for timely Hunchback shutoff, and prolonged Hunchback repeats lineage-specific first-born features.
cards.quote: Another factor, Seven-up, is needed to switch Hunchback off on time
cards.section: Seven-up times the switch

cards.front: A ferret layer-4-stage donor produces upper-layer daughters in an older host but fails to produce layer-6 daughters in a younger host. Does the failure imply that its laminar fate was already completely fixed?
cards.back: No. Upper-layer output demonstrates retained ability to shift forward; failure to make layer 6 instead supports selective loss of earlier competence.
cards.quote: ferret progenitors at an intermediate stage, making layer 4, could be pushed forward to upper layers but not back to layer 6.
cards.section: Intermediate-stage grafts

cards.front: Late mouse apical progenitors can regain earlier states in young hosts through Wnt sensing, but intermediate progenitors do not. How should this change a claim that ferret grafts prove irreversible competence loss in every cortical progenitor?
cards.back: Restrict the claim. Ferret grafts support narrowing in their tested population, while the mouse result shows that reversal depends on progenitor type and cues. Combining both rules, narrowing is the normal course rather than a universal law.
cards.quote: late apical progenitors moved into younger hosts can return to earlier states by sensing Wnt, while intermediate progenitors cannot
cards.section: How some mouse progenitors go back

cards.front: The modeled mouse ventricular-zone Q schedule spans eleven cycles over six days. Using 24 hours per day, what average cycle duration is implied, and is it consistent with the stated change from about 8 to about 18 hours?
cards.back: Total time ≈ 6 × 24 = 144 hours. Mean cycle duration ≈ 144/11 = 13.1 hours, within the stated early-to-late range of about 8–18 hours; individual cycles need not equal the mean.
cards.quote: The cell cycle lengthens over the same days, from about 8 hours early to about 18 hours late.
cards.section: Timing the Q schedule

cards.front: Why shouldn't the medial ganglionic eminence's inside-out birthdate rule be generalized to all cortical interneurons?
cards.back: Caudal ganglionic eminence interneurons go mainly to superficial layers, and their layer follows birth date less closely.
cards.quote: Interneurons from the caudal ganglionic eminence go mainly to superficial layers, and their layer follows birth date less closely
cards.section: Interneurons in transplants, and those that do not follow the rule
